rules.title: Ban on retaliatory termination, rent increase, or change in tenancy terms
rules.requirement: A landlord may not threaten or take reprisals, including termination notices or rent increases, against a tenant for reporting code violations, taking legal action under housing laws, complaining in writing to the landlord, or organizing or joining a tenants' union. A termination notice (except for nonpayment), rent increase, or major change in terms within six months of such activity is presumed retaliatory, and the tenant can recover 1 to 3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees.
rules.key_value: 6-month rebuttable presumption of reprisal; damages 1–3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants of residential premises in Massachusetts; applies to any person or agent who threatens or takes reprisals.
rules.exemptions: Termination notices for nonpayment of rent do not trigger the presumption.
rules.quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action
rules.penalty: Damages of not less than one month's rent or more than three months' rent, or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees; any waiver in a lease is void.

notes: The document is M.G.L. c. 186, § 18, the Massachusetts anti-retaliation statute. It isn't a full just-cause eviction law: landlords can still end a tenancy for any non-retaliatory reason. It does limit the reasons for ending a tenancy, though, by barring reprisal, so I filed it under just_cause_eviction with reduced confidence (0.6). A reviewer may decide to leave it out of scope. It also touches rent increases, since a retaliatory increase is presumed to be a reprisal, but it sets no cap, so I didn't make a separate rent_increase_limits record. The page gives no effective date, so I left it null and marked the rule in_force as a long-standing General Law.
